    About this catalogue

    A scrollable, self-contained reference of biological sequences — DNA, RNA and protein — for living things other than humans, with each sequence rendered as text, as binary, and as mathematics.

    Entries come only from documents you import (FASTA, GenBank, PDB seqres, plain bases, gzipped or not). Nothing is invented. Every derived number is shown beside the formula that produced it. Identical sequences are merged into one entry that lists all the records it came from.

    Organism names are attached when the source carries them. PDB seqres files carry none, so those entries sit under organism unknown until you import a chain-to-taxonomy table (SIFTS pdb_chain_taxonomy.tsv); after that, one button removes everything marked Homo sapiens.

    Large corpora render lazily: the contents list on the left is paged, and an entry's full article opens when you tap it. With a small catalogue everything is opened at once, wiki-style. / focuses search.

    Where the real 3D anatomy of an organism, or the atomic fold of a protein, is not in the file, the catalogue does not pretend: it says so on the entry and offers the geometric models it can justify.

    This file carries its own corpus: every DNA/RNA chain from the wwPDB seqres release you supplied (20,009 unique sequences, mounted at load) and every protein chain (185,891 unique sequences, kept packed until you ask — unpacking needs about 1 GB of memory and is desktop-only). Every entry has 3D models: a helix built from crystallographic parameters for nucleic acids, and superformula bodies for form, all exportable as OBJ.

    Species come from the Catalogue of Life [14]: import any COL download (TextTree, ColDP NameUsage.tsv, or Darwin Core Taxon.tsv, gzipped or not) and the sidebar becomes a species list. Every sequence with an organism name is paired to its species automatically; sequences without one wait under loose sequences until you pair them or import a taxonomy table. With the file online, each species page can fetch its own reference DNA from NCBI GenBank [15].

    No entries yet. Press Import and paste or drop a sequence file.

    Method & formulas

    Alphabets

    DNA: A, C, G, T; RNA uses U for T [1]. Proteins: the 20 standard amino acids, one letter each; X marks an unknown residue. IUPAC ambiguity codes (N, R, Y…) are kept in the text lane and masked in the binary lane.

    Binary translation

    Nucleic, 2-bit: A → 00 C → 01 G → 10 T/U → 11 (4 bases per byte, first base high) Protein, 5-bit: index in ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY, 0..19 → 5 bits; X → 11111 ASCII, 8-bit: plain code of each letter, for comparison

    Nucleic acid composition

    GC% = (G+C)/N GC skew = (G−C)/(G+C) AT skew = (A−T)/(A+T) Chargaff: A≈T and G≈C for double-stranded DNA [3]; deviation reported, not assumed H₁ = −Σ p log₂ p over bases (max 2 bits); H₂ over dinucleotides (max 4 bits) Mass (ssDNA) ≈ 313.2A + 289.2C + 329.2G + 304.2T − 61.96 g/mol Tm (Wallace) N<14: 2(A+T)+4(G+C); N≥14: 64.9 + 41(G+C−16.4)/N

    Protein composition

    Mass ≈ Σ residue masses + 18.02 (water) GRAVY = mean Kyte–Doolittle hydropathy (positive = hydrophobic) Net charge at pH 7 ≈ (K + R) − (D + E) (His neutral) H₁ = −Σ p log₂ p over residues (max log₂20 = 4.32 bits) Hydropathy curve: 9-residue sliding window of Kyte–Doolittle values

    Sequence as a curve

    Chaos Game Representation (Jeffrey 1990): corners A=(0,0) C=(0,1) G=(1,1) T=(1,0); pᵢ = (pᵢ₋₁ + corner)/2 Z-curve (Zhang 1994): xₙ=(A+G)−(C+T), yₙ=(A+C)−(G+T), zₙ=(A+T)−(G+C)

    Translation

    Standard genetic code (table 1), three forward frames, ORFs counted from ATG to the next stop. RNA is read as if U = T.

    3D models

    Nucleic helix (per base i, angle θ = 2π·i / bp-per-turn, height z = i · rise): strand 1: (R cos θ, R sin θ, z) strand 2 (DNA): (R cos(θ+2.2), R sin(θ+2.2), z) B-DNA: 10.5 bp/turn, rise 3.38 Å, R 10 Å [3] A-RNA: 11 bp/turn, rise 2.55 Å, R 11.5 Å [3] Rendered as backbone polylines with base-pair rungs; exported OBJ is in ångströms. 3D superformula (spherical product, Gielis 2003 [10]): x = r₁(θ) cos θ · r₂(φ) cos φ, y = r₁(θ) sin θ · r₂(φ) cos φ, z = r₂(φ) sin φ θ ∈ [−π, π], φ ∈ [−π/2, π/2]; r₁, r₂ are 2D superformulas with (m, n₁, n₂, n₃) Exported OBJ is a 24×48 quad mesh, normalised to the unit cube.

    Form & shape

    A sequence does not encode a silhouette you can read off directly, so two things are kept apart: a form genome (superformula parameters seeded from the sequence statistics — repeatable, distinct, but a visual hash, not anatomy) and an editable form model (Gielis superformula for radial bodies, L-system for branching bodies) that you fill in to describe the real organism.

    r(φ) = ( |cos(mφ/4)/a|^n₂ + |sin(mφ/4)/b|^n₃ )^(−1/n₁) L-system: F forward, ± turn θ, [ ] push/pop

    Import

    Drop files here (.fasta .gb .txt .gz .tsv .fweddle, or a Catalogue of Life TextTree / NameUsage.tsv / Taxon.tsv), or

    Large files (the full PDB seqres is 400 MB) stream in and are merged by identical sequence. That import is desktop-only in practice; on a phone, open a pre-built .fweddle capsule instead.
